title: Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review
authors: Saw AE, Main LC, Gastin PB
population: Athletes in 56 original studies reporting concurrent subjective and objective well-being measures
findings: Fifty-six original studies reported concurrent subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being; the two generally did not correlate.
Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training loads with superior sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.
Subjective well-being was typically impaired with an acute increase in training load and with chronic training, while an acute decrease in training load improved it.
Subjective measures may stand alone or be incorporated into a mixed-methods approach to athlete monitoring.
56 original studies reporting concurrent subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being were evaluated for levels of evidence (databases searched May 2014).
Subjective and objective measures of well-being generally did not correlate.
Subjective well-being was typically impaired with an acute increase in training load and with chronic training, while an acute decrease in load improved it.
Authors support subjective measures standing alone or within a mixed-methods monitoring approach.
limitations: Mixed sports and measures; no pooled effect sizes in the abstract; levels of evidence were assessed qualitatively. Not specific to runners.
implications: Include a brief daily or per-run subjective check-in (fatigue, sleep, soreness, mood, readiness) as a first-class input to load adjustments.

Because subjective and objective measures often disagree, a single subjective decline may trim the next hard session, but require two independent signals before auto-inserting an unplanned recovery week (design choice).
Make a short daily subjective wellness rating (fatigue, sleep quality, soreness, mood, stress) the primary readiness input and treat HRV/resting HR as secondary.
Because subjective and objective markers rarely agree, do not change the plan on a single objective marker alone.
Track the subjective trend over days, since the signal is about response to load.

verification.notes: Crossref issued 2015 (online 9 Sep 2015); journal issue is Br J Sports Med 2016;50(5):281-91, so year 2016 retained. Findings verified against PubMed abstract.
